steps.title: Oxidation
steps.body: An oxidised wine has lost its fresh fruit, smelling of bruised apple, sherry or nuts, with browning colour. It comes from too much contact with oxygen, through a faulty closure, poor storage or careless winemaking. It's a fault in a fresh white, but a deliberate style in Oloroso or tawny Port. Acetaldehyde is the main compound.

steps.title: Reduction
steps.body: Reduction is the opposite: too little oxygen, in a wine with sulphur compounds. It smells of rotten egg, struck match, rubber or cabbage. Hydrogen sulphide, the rotten egg smell, forms when stressed yeast lacks nutrients. Light reduction, struck match, can add complexity in some whites; strong reduction is a fault.

steps.prompt: Match each smell to its cause.
steps.explanation: Each fault has a typical smell.

steps.title: What to do
steps.body: Some reduction can be fixed by air: decanting or swirling may blow off struck match or rubber. Persistent rotten egg can sometimes be cleared by a clean copper coin, which binds sulphides. Oxidation can't be undone. Screw caps, which let in little oxygen, can sometimes favour reduction; corks can favour oxidation.
steps.highlight: Air can help reduction, not oxidation

steps.prompt: Which could be signs of oxidation in a young white?
steps.explanation: Fresh lime and green apple are signs of a sound, youthful white.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Oxidation brings bruised apple, browning and loss of fruit
Reduction brings rotten egg, rubber or struck match
Air can fix mild reduction; oxidation is permanent
